title: The Grandfather's Library to the Boulevard du Montparnasse: Sartre, the Freedom Nobody Asked For
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Paris, 13 rue Mignard: the fatherless start
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rue_Mignard states the philosopher was born 21 June 1905 at number 13. Coordinates taken from the French Wikipedia article on the street (48 51 49 N, 2 16 28 E) rather than from the research pool's original pin, which sat some 230 metres east of the street.
stops.campa: In the sixteenth arrondissement, on a short street running from the avenue Henri-Martin to the rue de Siam, Anne-Marie Schweitzer gives birth to a son at number 13, on the twenty-first of June. They name him Jean-Paul Charles Aymard. His father Jean-Baptiste is a naval officer who has brought a fever home from Indochina and has some fifteen months left to live. The boy will be an only child, small, with a wandering eye. In the house he is raised in, the missing man is mentioned politely and seldom. The father dies before the son is old enough to have a memory of him.
suggested_refs: 13 rue Mignard, quartier de la Muette, Paris 16e

stops.name: Meudon, the house of Charles Schweitzer
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year of the father's death and the move; the month and day are not given by the sources and default to 01-01.
stops.campa: His father dead, his mother takes him back to her parents, and the raising of Jean-Paul passes to Charles Schweitzer, a teacher of languages with a white beard and a library. The grandfather does not send the boy to school at first. He sets him among the books instead, and the boy reads before he properly plays. Anne-Marie is treated in that house as an elder sister rather than as a mother. Out of this arrangement come both the writer's vocation and the account of it he will publish nearly sixty years later under the title Les Mots.
suggested_refs: The Schweitzer house at Meudon; Charles Schweitzer's library

stops.name: La Rochelle, the stepfather's town
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia gives 26 April 1917 for the relocation following his mother's remarriage.
stops.campa: Anne-Marie remarries, and the household moves to the Atlantic port where her new husband works. Sartre is eleven, undersized, cross-eyed, and newly out of reach of his grandfather's protection. The boys at the lycée in La Rochelle beat him. He lies to them, invents feats, tries to buy their attention; none of it holds. The ramparts, the harbour and the fishing fleet leave no mark on anything he ever writes. The schoolyard does. The war is in its third year and its front lies far to the north and east of this coast.
suggested_refs: The lycée at La Rochelle, 1917-1920

stops.name: Paris, Lycée Henri-IV: back on the mountain
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; the month is inferred from the French school calendar and the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: The family puts him back into Paris, at the Lycée Henri-IV on the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève, and the three years of La Rochelle close behind him. He is fifteen. Here he takes up again what the grandfather's library began, and he means to be a writer; the ambition is not vague, it is a schedule. He works at Greek, at Latin, at philosophy, with the others who mean to sit the entrance examination for the rue d'Ulm. The school he is preparing for stands five hundred metres down the hill, and he will spend the next decade inside that half-kilometre.
suggested_refs: Lycée Henri-IV, Paris 5e
Cours Hattemer, his earlier Paris schooling

stops.name: École Normale Supérieure, 45 rue d'Ulm: the entrance
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year of entry; month inferred from the school calendar, day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He enters the École Normale Supérieure in 1924, one of the small cohort the Third Republic trains to teach philosophy to itself. Raymond Aron and Paul Nizan are in the same house. The school gives him four years of reading, arguing, drinking, and elaborate practical jokes, and the standing of a clown who is also the cleverest man in the room. In 1928 he completes a thesis on the image in psychological life under Henri Delacroix. Then he fails the agrégation at the first attempt, which surprises everyone including him, and sits down to prepare it again.
suggested_refs: École Normale Supérieure, 45 rue d'Ulm
Sartre's 1928 diplome, 'L'Image dans la vie psychologique'

stops.name: The Sorbonne and the Louvre bench: first and second
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1929 results and the pact; the pin is the canonical Sorbonne/Louvre coordinate already used in simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json and is inherited unchanged. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: At the second attempt he places first in the agrégation de philosophie. Second place goes to Simone de Beauvoir, twenty-one years old, the youngest candidate ever to pass it. That autumn the two of them make a pact on a bench outside the Louvre: an essential love between them, contingent loves permitted elsewhere, nothing concealed from each other, and no marriage. For fifty years people will refuse to believe the terms were meant literally. Neither of the two breaks them.
suggested_refs: The 1929 agrégation de philosophie results
The pact of 1929, as recounted in Beauvoir's memoirs

stops.name: Le Havre, Lycée François-Ier: the port he cannot stand
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia gives March 1931 to 1936 for the Le Havre posting. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Assigned to the Lycée François-Ier at Le Havre in March 1931, he teaches philosophy to the sons of shipowners and clerks in a port town he privately despises. He is twenty-five and has published nothing. He fills a notebook about a man called Antoine Roquentin who discovers that things are simply there, in excess, for no reason at all. Le Havre goes into the book as Bouville. He stays five years, correcting exercises, walking the docks in winter, and posting chapters to Paris under the title Melancholia.
suggested_refs: Lycée François-Ier, Le Havre
The manuscript titled Melancholia, later La Nausée

stops.name: Bec de Gaz, Montparnasse: Aron names the thing
stops.date_confidence: attested as an episode by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, which dates it to the early 1930s; the year 1932 is the pool's dating and the month and day default to 01-01. The pin is the Montparnasse bar's approximate location.
stops.campa: Raymond Aron, back from a year in Berlin, drinks with Sartre and Beauvoir at a Montparnasse bar they call the Bec de Gaz. Aron points at the glass in front of him and explains what a phenomenologist may do with it. Sartre goes pale. Everything he has been trying to do in fiction for six years, and cannot do in the philosophy he was trained in, is suddenly available as a method: describe the thing as it appears, and do not go behind it. Within a year he has arranged to take Aron's own post in Berlin.
stops.quote: you see, mon petit camarade, if you are a phenomenologist you can talk about this cocktail and that is philosophy
stops.quote_source: Raymond Aron to Sartre at the Bec de Gaz, Montparnasse, reported in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Sartre'
suggested_refs: The Bec de Gaz, Montparnasse
Husserl's Ideen and Logische Untersuchungen, Aron's Berlin reading

stops.name: Berlin, Institut français d'Allemagne: a year inside Husserl
stops.date_confidence: attested for the academic year 1933-34; the research pool's original pin for the institute could not be verified against any source naming its Berlin address, so the canonical Berlin coordinate already used in simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json is inherited instead. Month inferred, day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He succeeds Raymond Aron at the Institut français d'Allemagne and spends the academic year reading Husserl in the city where Hitler has just taken power. By his own later account he attends to the politics less than he should have. What he carries out of the year is a conviction that consciousness has no inside: it is a bursting outward toward things, with no ego lodged behind it. Beauvoir comes out to join him in 1934. The essay that makes the case, La Transcendance de l'ego, is drafted here.
suggested_refs: Institut français d'Allemagne, Berlin, 1933-34
Husserl, Ideen I

stops.name: Laon, Lycée de Laon: the transcendence of the ego
stops.date_confidence: attested for the school year 1936-37; en.wikipedia names the Lycée de Laon, correcting the research pool, which had him at the École normale d'instituteurs. Month inferred from the school calendar, day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Posted to the lycée at Laon for the school year, he teaches on the ridge above the plain of Picardy, under the cathedral with the stone oxen in its towers, ninety miles from Paris and three years from the war. La Transcendance de l'ego is published the same year: consciousness is impersonal, the I is an object it constitutes like any other, and the self is out in the world among the chestnut trees, available to anyone who looks. He is thirty-one and has still published no book. On free days he takes the train to Paris.
suggested_refs: Lycée de Laon, 1936-37
La Transcendance de l'ego (1936)

stops.name: Neuilly-sur-Seine, Lycée Pasteur: La Nausée in the shops
stops.date_confidence: the Neuilly posting is attested from 1937 to 1939 and La Nausée is attested to 1938; the month is inferred to place the publication inside the posting and the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He is transferred to the Lycée Pasteur at Neuilly, on the western edge of Paris, and Gallimard brings out the Le Havre notebook as La Nausée. The publisher has made him drop the title Melancholia. Roquentin, in a café in Bouville, finds that existence is not a category but a substance, that it sticks, that it is in the purple suspenders of the man at the next table. The book is a success and the teacher of philosophy becomes a novelist in one season. Le Mur is published the following year, in 1939.
stops.quote: The Nausea is not inside me: I feel it out there in the wall, in the suspenders, everywhere around me.
stops.quote_source: La Nausée (1938), trans. Lloyd Alexander, New Directions; the entry headed 'Friday'
suggested_refs: La Nausée, Gallimard, 1938
Le Mur, Gallimard, 1939
sources: archive.org item 'nausea-jean-paul-sartre' (Lloyd Alexander translation, full text)

stops.name: Paris, the station: mobilised, 2 September 1939
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pin is the Paris station coordinate already used in simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json for this same departure and is inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: On the second of September 1939, the day before France declares war, Sartre leaves Paris by train with his kit. He is thirty-four, a lycée teacher with two books out and a third promised, and the army has assigned him to the meteorological service on account of his eye. He will not fire a shot in the whole of this war. Neither he nor Beauvoir expects the twenty months that follow, or a war at all in the sense the word is about to acquire. She sees him off from the platform.
suggested_refs: The mobilisation orders of 2 September 1939

stops.name: Alsace, the meteorological post: measuring the wind
stops.date_confidence: attested that he served as a meteorologist and that the Stanford entry names Alsace as the sector; no precise station is documented, and the pin is the sector's principal city. Month and day are ordering devices only.
stops.campa: His war consists of releasing balloons, reading the wind off them, and telephoning the figures to an artillery unit that may or may not use them. He calls it afterwards the idlest stretch of his life. He fills notebook after notebook: on time, on bad faith, on Heidegger, on what a man is supposed to do with a freedom he cannot hand back. The treatise he publishes in 1943 has its foundations in these months. He is a private soldier in a village behind the Rhine, and between weather reports there is nothing to do.
suggested_refs: Les Carnets de la drôle de guerre, the 1939-40 war notebooks

stops.name: Padoux, Vosges: taken prisoner on his birthday
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padoux states that Sartre was arrested by the Germans at Padoux on 21 June 1940 while serving as a soldier-meteorologist. The Stanford entry's 'Alsace' refers to his posting sector, not to the place of capture, and is not a competing account of this event. Coordinates corrected to the commune's own (48 16 51 N, 6 34 14 E), some 8.5 km from the pool's original pin.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of June 1940, the day he turns thirty-five, German troops take him at Padoux in the Vosges. He has spent nine months measuring the weather for an army that has now ceased to exist, and he has not fired a shot in the whole of it. He walks into captivity on his own birthday, carrying the notebooks and whatever a soldier is allowed to keep. The roads of Lorraine that week are full of columns moving in both directions at once. The armistice is signed the following day.
suggested_refs: Padoux, Vosges, the commune where the capture is recorded

stops.name: Stalag XII-D, Trier: Bariona at Christmas
stops.date_confidence: the captivity at Nancy and then Stalag XII-D near Trier is attested, as is the composition and camp performance of Bariona; the Christmas 1940 date follows from the play being a Nativity piece staged for the camp, and the exact day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He is held first at Nancy, then at Stalag XII-D outside Trier, among some twenty-five thousand men. The camp gives him something the rue d'Ulm never did: a collective in which a priest, a communist, and a philosopher draw the same ration. At Christmas he writes a Nativity play, Bariona ou le fils du tonnerre, and the prisoners stage it for the camp. The censors read scripture. The prisoners hear a country under occupation being told to rise. It is the first play he writes. He is released in April on grounds of poor health.
suggested_refs: Bariona, ou le fils du tonnerre, written and staged at Stalag XII-D, Christmas 1940

stops.name: Paris, Lycée Condorcet: the chair that was made vacant
stops.date_confidence: attested as to October 1941 and as to the previous holder having been a Jewish teacher removed under Vichy law; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: In October 1941 he takes the khâgne at the Lycée Condorcet. The chair is open because the man who held it, a Jew, has been struck off under Vichy law. Sartre takes it, and will be asked about it for the rest of his life. He has by then founded and effectively lost Socialisme et Liberté, the resistance group he ran with Beauvoir and Merleau-Ponty. It printed tracts, recruited some dozens of people, and could not survive contact with the networks that were doing the real thing.
suggested_refs: Lycée Condorcet, Paris 9e
Socialisme et Liberté, 1941

stops.name: Café de Flore, boulevard Saint-Germain: writing where it is warm
stops.date_confidence: the habit is attested across the Occupation years rather than to a single date; the year 1942 is an ordering device and the day defaults to 01. The pin is the Café de Flore coordinate already used in simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json and is inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: There is no coal. The Flore has a stove and its owner keeps it lit, so Sartre and Beauvoir arrive when the doors open and work at the same two tables until they close, using a boulevard Saint-Germain café as an office because their rooms cannot be heated. A great deal of the philosophy of freedom is written here, in pencil, in a public room in an occupied city. The waiters take their messages. The other regulars are actors, poets, black marketeers, and at least one informer.
suggested_refs: Café de Flore, 172 boulevard Saint-Germain
Les Deux Magots, a few doors away, associated with the same circle

stops.name: Paris, Cahiers du Sud: reviewing L'Étranger
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1943; the pin is the Paris coordinate already used in albert_camus.journey.json for this episode and is inherited unchanged. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: In February 1943 he gives a long article in Cahiers du Sud to a novel published the previous June by a tubercular Algerian journalist he has not yet met. He takes L'Étranger seriously and takes it apart, and the review makes Albert Camus a name in Paris. From then on the two are quoted together, photographed together, and paired by every journalist in France, an arrangement neither of them enjoys and neither refuses. Camus comes north that autumn, joins the clandestine Combat network, and walks into the same circle.
suggested_refs: Sartre, 'Explication de L'Étranger', Cahiers du Sud, February 1943

stops.name: Paris, Gallimard: L'Être et le néant
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1943 by both the Stanford Encyclopedia and Wikipedia; the month is the conventional June date and the day defaults to 01. The pin is the Gallimard coordinate already used in simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json.
stops.campa: Gallimard publishes seven hundred pages of ontology in the middle of the Occupation. Consciousness is a hole in being; it is what it is not and is not what it is; freedom is not a property a man has but the condition he cannot get out of, which is why it is unbearable. Bad faith is the lie told to oneself in order to escape it. The waiter who is a little too much a waiter is in it. So is the woman who leaves her hand where it was put and decides not to notice. He is thirty-eight.
stops.quote: man is the being by whom Nothingness comes into the world
stops.quote_source: L'Être et le néant (1943), trans. Hazel Barnes, Introduction
suggested_refs: L'Être et le néant, Gallimard, 1943
Hazel Barnes's 1956 translation; Sarah Richmond's 2018 retranslation

stops.name: Paris, the occupied stage: Les Mouches and Huis clos
stops.date_confidence: Les Mouches is attested to 1943 and Huis clos to 1944; the two are held in one stop and dated to the later premiere. The precise day is an ordering device. The pin is the canonical Paris coordinate inherited from albert_camus.journey.json and simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json, the individual theatres not being separately pinned.
stops.campa: Les Mouches goes up in 1943 with the German censor's approval: an Orestes who kills and refuses to repent, in a city where everybody in the stalls who wants to read that as occupied France reads it so. In May 1944, weeks before the landings, Huis clos opens. The sentence the whole century will quote is spoken in it by a coward called Garcin. Three dead people are locked in a Second Empire drawing room with the lights on, no mirrors, no eyelids, and no torturer, because none is required.
stops.quote_source: Huis clos (1944), Garcin's line, in the standard English translation
suggested_refs: Huis clos, premiere 1944
Les Mouches, staged 1943
sources: the line itself is tagged [R]: no readable full text of the play could be reached to verify it against the primary text

stops.name: Paris, Gallimard: the review takes its name
stops.date_confidence: attested: the review took shape at Gallimard under Sartre's direction in October 1944, was named in December 1944, and its first issue appeared in October 1945. The Stanford Encyclopedia's founding date of 1943 is not supported by any other source consulted and is not carried here as a live contradiction. The pin is the Gallimard coordinate inherited from simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json.
stops.campa: The review takes shape at Gallimard through the autumn of 1944 and is given its name in December. Sartre directs it; the committee around him includes Beauvoir and Merleau-Ponty. For the next thirty-five years the political position of French intellectual life is largely settled in these offices, and so are a good many of its quarrels. The first issue reaches the kiosks in October 1945, announcing a literature that is engaged, answerable, written from inside a situation and addressed to a public that has to act.
suggested_refs: Les Temps modernes, first issue, October 1945
Sartre's 'Présentation des Temps modernes'

stops.name: Salle des Centraux, rue Montgolfier: the lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to the evening of 29 October 1945, at half past eight, before an audience assembled by the Club Maintenant.
stops.campa: At half past eight in the evening, in a hall on the rue Montgolfier hired by the Club Maintenant, more people arrive than the room holds and the crowd presses at the doors. Sartre has come to answer the charge that his philosophy is a counsel of despair. He argues instead that it is the only optimism on offer, since it leaves a man nothing outside himself to blame and no nature to fall back on. The lecture is printed the next year and becomes the most read thing he ever wrote. He regrets it for the next thirty-five years.
stops.quote: What they have in common is simply the fact that they believe that existence comes before essence.
stops.quote_source: L'existentialisme est un humanisme, the lecture of 29 October 1945, English translation at marxists.org
suggested_refs: L'Existentialisme est un humanisme, Nagel, 1946

stops.name: 42 rue Bonaparte: the apartment of the loud years
stops.date_confidence: attested that he held the apartment from 1945 to 1962; the entry date here is an ordering device inside that span and the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He takes an apartment at 42 rue Bonaparte, above the square where the Flore and the Deux Magots face each other, and keeps it for seventeen years. His mother lives there with him for part of them. Out of these rooms come the last of the Chemins de la liberté, Réflexions sur la question juive, Qu'est-ce que la littérature, Les mains sales, Saint Genet, the Critique de la raison dialectique, and a volume of political journalism most years. The bell rings all day. He answers, on principle, nearly every letter that comes.
suggested_refs: 42 rue Bonaparte, Paris 6e, 1945-1962

stops.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés: the letters that end it
stops.date_confidence: attested: Camus published L'Homme révolté in 1951, Francis Jeanson's hostile review appeared in Les Temps modernes in May 1952, and the exchange of open letters between Camus and Sartre ran in the August 1952 issue. The pin is inherited unchanged from albert_camus.journey.json. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Camus publishes L'Homme révolté in 1951, against revolutionary murder and against the men who write the justifications for it. Sartre gives the book to Francis Jeanson, who takes it apart in Les Temps modernes in May. Camus answers in August, addressing his reply not to Jeanson but to Monsieur le Directeur, and Sartre answers him in the same issue, at length, in public, for keeps. They do not speak again. Camus is thirty-eight that year and Sartre is forty-seven.
suggested_refs: Les Temps modernes, May 1952 (Jeanson) and August 1952 (the Camus-Sartre exchange)

stops.name: Beijing, the state visit
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955 by the Beauvoir article, which records the pair being photographed in Beijing; the month and day are ordering devices only.
stops.campa: Sartre and Beauvoir travel to the People's Republic and are shown what visiting writers are shown. He is fifty, and he has decided by now that a Western intellectual who attacks the communist world without attacking his own is doing police work for his own government. The position has already cost him Camus, and it costs him Merleau-Ponty. He had visited the Soviet Union the year before, after Stalin's death. The photographs from these years show him smiling in crowds, at a distance, in the middle of a delegation.
suggested_refs: The 1955 Sartre and Beauvoir visit to Maoist China
Sartre's 1954 visit to the Soviet Union

stops.name: Paris, Le fantôme de Staline: Budapest
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1956. The research pool's phrasing that he 'broke with the French Communist Party' is corrected here: he was never a member, but a fellow traveller from 1952, and the rupture was with a party he had been allied to. Pin is the canonical Paris coordinate; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Soviet tanks enter Budapest in November 1956. Sartre, who has never carried a party card and has spent four years defending the French Communists as a fellow traveller, publishes Le fantôme de Staline in Les Temps modernes and breaks with them in public. He does not become an anti-communist. What he becomes is harder to place: a man who denounces his allies without going over to their enemies, and who will do it again at intervals for the rest of his life. He is fifty-one.
stops.quote: For them I wasn't a whole man; I was a dead man on reprieve.
stops.quote_source: 'A Fellow Traveler of the Communist Party' (1972), Sartre on how the PCF regarded non-member allies
suggested_refs: 'Le fantôme de Staline', Les Temps modernes, 1956-57

stops.name: Paris, the obituary for Camus
stops.date_confidence: Camus died at Villeblevin on 4 January 1960 and was buried at Lourmarin on 6 January; Sartre's obituary was written in Paris, and the day given here is an ordering device between those two dates. Villeblevin and Lourmarin are Camus's own stops and are not staged here.
stops.campa: Camus dies on the fourth of January in a car on a straight road near Villeblevin, with an unused train ticket in his pocket. Two days later he is buried at Lourmarin, in the Vaucluse, and Sartre is not there. Sartre, who has not spoken to him in eight years, writes the obituary. He does not withdraw a word of the quarrel and he does not pretend the friendship survived it. He writes about the work, and about a line of French moralists that Camus is described as inheriting.
stops.quote: the present heir of that long line of moralists whose works constitute perhaps what is most original in French letters
stops.quote_source: Sartre's published obituary for Albert Camus, January 1960
suggested_refs: Sartre's obituary of Camus, January 1960

stops.name: Havana, with Guevara
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1960; the month and day are ordering devices. The photographs with Che Guevara and Antonio Núñez Jiménez are the documented record of the visit.
stops.campa: Sartre and Beauvoir go to Cuba in the first year of the revolutionary government and are received as its guests. He talks at length with Che Guevara, who is thirty-one and running the national bank, and is photographed with him and with the geographer Antonio Núñez Jiménez. Everything he sees is young and improvised and not yet an institution, which is the condition his philosophy is built to admire. It is the same year he finishes the first volume of the Critique de la raison dialectique.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Sartre, Beauvoir, Guevara and Núñez Jiménez, Havana 1960

stops.name: Paris, Gallimard: Critique de la raison dialectique
stops.date_confidence: volume one is attested to 1960; the month is an ordering device and the day defaults to 01. The research pool paired this with a 1960 staging of Les Séquestrés d'Altona; the play in fact premiered on 23 September 1959 at the Théâtre de la Renaissance, and the two are separated here.
stops.campa: Volume one of the Critique de la raison dialectique appears: some seven hundred and fifty pages trying to fit a philosophy of freedom inside a Marxism with no room for one. The individual project, the practico-inert, the group in fusion that forms at the Bastille and hardens back into an institution. He is attempting to say how men make history and are then made out of it. Volume two is left unfinished and appears five years after his death. The previous autumn Les Séquestrés d'Altona had opened at the Théâtre de la Renaissance.
stops.quote: In our view Philosophy does not exist.
stops.quote_source: 'Marxism and Existentialism', the opening study of the Critique de la raison dialectique (1960), first paragraph
suggested_refs: Critique de la raison dialectique, vol. 1, Gallimard, 1960
Les Séquestrés d'Altona, premiere 23 September 1959

stops.name: Paris, the Manifeste des 121 and the Jeanson trial
stops.date_confidence: the Manifeste des 121 is attested to September 1960 and the letter to the Jeanson network's trial to the same year; the day given is the manifesto's publication date and is used here to order the segment. Pin is the canonical Paris coordinate.
stops.campa: A hundred and twenty-one writers, film-makers and academics sign a declaration on the right of insubordination in the Algerian war, and Sartre is among them. Signing is a criminal act. In the same season he writes to the court trying the Jeanson network, French men and women who carried money and false papers for the FLN, and puts himself in writing on their side of the dock. Careers end over this. Sartre holds no post that anyone can take away from him.
stops.quote: For the first time, despite all obstacles, all prejudices, Algerians and Frenchmen, fraternally united in a common combat, find themselves together in the box of the accused.
stops.quote_source: Letter in Support of the Jeanson Network (1960)
suggested_refs: Le Manifeste des 121, September 1960
The Jeanson network trial, Paris, September 1960

stops.name: Paris, the preface for Fanon
stops.date_confidence: the preface is attested to 1961, the year of the book's publication and of Fanon's death in December; the month and day are ordering devices. Pin is the canonical Paris coordinate.
stops.campa: Frantz Fanon, a Martinican psychiatrist working out of Tunis and dying of leukaemia, asks Sartre for a preface to Les Damnés de la terre. Sartre writes one that turns on the European reader and refuses him the seat of a spectator. The humanism of the metropole is described in it as a cover story; colonial violence is described as coming back to the men who invented it and using their own vocabulary. The preface is more famous, and more attacked, than most of the book behind it. Fanon dies in December, aged thirty-six.
stops.quote: In the notion of the human race we found an abstract assumption of universality which served as cover for the most realistic practices.
stops.quote_source: Preface to Frantz Fanon, Les Damnés de la terre (1961)
suggested_refs: Sartre's preface to Les Damnés de la terre, Maspero, 1961

stops.name: 42 rue Bonaparte: the plastic bomb at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1961 by en.wikipedia, which also records a second attack the following year and threatening letters arriving from Oran. The research pool's July dating is corrected. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: In June 1961 a plastic charge goes off in the entrance of his building on the rue Bonaparte. Partisans of French Algeria have been sending him threatening letters from Oran for months, and he has kept writing. What he had written about France was that it no longer frightened anyone and had begun instead to horrify, and the men who set the charges are among the people who had read it. A second charge follows the next year. He leaves the apartment then, after sixteen years in the same rooms above the same square.
stops.quote: France frightens no one; it no longer even has the means to intimidate: it's beginning to horrify, and that is all.
stops.quote_source: 'We Are All Assassins' (1958), written on the Fernand Yveton case and the bombing of Sakiet
suggested_refs: The two attacks on 42 rue Bonaparte, 1961 and 1962

stops.name: Paris, Gallimard: Les Mots
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1964; the month and day default to 01-01. Pin is the Gallimard coordinate inherited from simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json.
stops.campa: He publishes the account of his own childhood: the grandfather's library, the small boy performing for adults, the discovery that a vocation had been handed to him the way another child is handed a name. The judgement is merciless, on the child and on the literature the child was promised. The book stops at the age of ten. In Stockholm the prize committees are reading it that summer. He announces afterwards that he has finished with fiction, and he keeps to it.
suggested_refs: Les Mots, Gallimard, 1964

stops.name: Paris, Le Figaro: the Nobel refused
stops.date_confidence: attested: the letter reached the Swedish Academy about a week before its final vote of 22 October 1964 and was disregarded; his statement appeared in Le Figaro on 23 October. Pin is the canonical Paris coordinate, the Stockholm side of the episode belonging to the Academy rather than to any journey Sartre made.
stops.campa: He writes to the Swedish Academy about a week before the vote, asking not to be considered. The letter arrives too late, or is set aside, and on the twenty-second of October they name him laureate anyway. The next day Le Figaro carries his statement: a writer who accepts an honour of this kind consents to become an institution, and he had refused the Légion d'honneur in 1945 on the same ground. He is the only person to have declined the prize in literature of his own accord. He never goes to Stockholm.
suggested_refs: Sartre's statement in Le Figaro, 23 October 1964
The Swedish Academy's deliberations of 22 October 1964

stops.name: Goxwiller, the Alsatian house: out of reach of the press
stops.date_confidence: attested that he went to ground at Hélène de Beauvoir's house in Goxwiller after the announcement; the exact day is an ordering device. Coordinates corrected to the commune's own (48 26 01 N, 7 29 07 E), some 4.3 km from the research pool's pin.
stops.campa: The press reaches the rue Bonaparte within hours and does not go away. Sartre goes east instead, to the Alsatian village where Beauvoir's sister Hélène keeps a house, and sits the noise out there among the vines under the Vosges. The prize money stays in Stockholm. Eleven years later the Academy's permanent secretary notes in his memoirs that somebody connected to Sartre had written to ask whether it was still available. That report is secondhand. It is also the only one there is.
suggested_refs: Hélène de Beauvoir's house at Goxwiller, Bas-Rhin
Lars Gyllensten's memoirs on the 1975 enquiry

stops.name: Paris, the adoption of Arlette Elkaïm
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1965 by the article on Arlette Elkaïm-Sartre, correcting the 1964 date carried elsewhere in the research pool; the month and day are ordering devices. Pin is the canonical Paris coordinate.
stops.campa: He formally adopts Arlette Elkaïm, an Algerian-born Jewish woman he met in 1956 when she was twenty-one, making her his legal daughter. She becomes, on his death, his universal legatee. The arrangement is explained to nobody and is not welcomed by everyone around him, Beauvoir included. It will decide which of Sartre's manuscripts are published after 1980, in what order, and edited by whom. No will can name that kind of authority over a body of work in so many words.
suggested_refs: The 1965 adoption; Arlette Elkaïm-Sartre's editorial work from 1985

stops.name: Stockholm, the Russell Tribunal
stops.date_confidence: attested that Sartre served as executive president of the 1967 tribunal, whose first session sat in Stockholm and whose second sat at Roskilde in Denmark; the research pool's 'Copenhagen' is corrected. The precise day orders the segment. Pin is the Stockholm coordinate already used in albert_camus.journey.json and is inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: Bertrand Russell, ninety-four, convenes a tribunal on American conduct in Vietnam and asks Sartre to preside. Sweden takes the first session; Denmark takes the second, at Roskilde, after France refuses the thing a venue at all. It has no state behind it, no power to compel a witness, no cell to put anyone in. It hears testimony for weeks from doctors, pilots, villagers and chemists. It returns a verdict of genocide. No court on earth is obliged to notice it.
suggested_refs: The Russell Tribunal, Stockholm and Roskilde sessions, 1967

stops.name: Paris, arrested in May
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was arrested for civil disobedience during the May 1968 unrest and released on de Gaulle's order; the day is an ordering device. The remark attributed to de Gaulle is tagged [R], reported rather than documented. Pin is the canonical Paris coordinate.
stops.campa: He is sixty-two when the students take the Sorbonne, and he goes to them rather than wait to be consulted. Of the eminent men of his generation invited to address the barricades, he is the one who goes. He speaks in the occupied lecture halls to a generation that has read Being and Nothingness at school. He is arrested for acts of civil disobedience during the May unrest, and let go on the order of Charles de Gaulle, who is reported to have said that one does not arrest Voltaire.
suggested_refs: The May 1968 occupations; Sartre's address in the occupied Sorbonne

stops.name: Goutte d'Or: the committee for Djellali Ben Ali
stops.date_confidence: attested for the winter of 1971; the month here reflects the killing of Djellali Ben Ali in late October and orders the stop. Note a live contradiction between two files in the corpus: gilles_deleuze.journey.json lists Deleuze as a co-signer of the Groupe d'Information sur les Prisons alongside Foucault, Sartre and Genet, while michel_foucault.journey.json names only Foucault, Vidal-Naquet and Domenach as founders. Not resolved here. Pin inherited unchanged from michel_foucault.journey.json.
stops.campa: A young Algerian, Djellali Ben Ali, is shot in the Goutte d'Or, and Sartre walks the quarter with Michel Foucault, Jean Genet and Claude Mauriac, setting up a committee of inquiry because the official one will not do the work. The same winter his name stands with Foucault's and Gilles Deleuze's on the Groupe d'Information sur les Prisons, which sends questionnaires into the jails and prints what comes back. He is sixty-six and half blind. What he still has to give is his name.
suggested_refs: The committee of inquiry into the killing of Djellali Ben Ali, winter 1971
Groupe d'Information sur les Prisons, 1971

stops.name: Paris, Gallimard: L'Idiot de la famille
stops.date_confidence: the first volumes are attested to 1971 and blindness to 1973; the month and day here are ordering devices. Pin is the Gallimard coordinate inherited from simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json.
stops.campa: The first volumes of a study of Gustave Flaubert appear, close to two thousand pages on a man dead since 1880, asking what can be known about a person if everything is brought against him at once: the family, the class, the century, the neurosis, the sentences. A third volume follows in 1972. The fourth is never written. In 1973 the eye that had been doing all the work for sixty-eight years fails, and Sartre, who has read every day of his life since Meudon, can no longer read.
suggested_refs: L'Idiot de la famille, Gallimard, 1971-1972
Flaubert's correspondence, Sartre's principal material

stops.name: Rome, the tape recorder
stops.date_confidence: tagged [R]: the Rome conversations of late summer 1974 are reported by the French Wikipedia article on Beauvoir and were not independently confirmed by a second source. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Sartre and Beauvoir spend the late summer in Rome. She sets a tape recorder between them and asks him, week after week, about his body, his childhood, his women, his politics, his reading and his death, and he answers all of it, including the parts that do him no credit. He cannot read the transcript back. The recordings become the second half of a book she publishes the year after he dies. In them the philosopher of freedom describes how little of it he has left.
suggested_refs: The 1974 Rome conversations, later published in La Cérémonie des adieux (1981)

stops.name: Paris, the last conversations
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1980 for the conversations with Benny Lévy, published as L'Espoir maintenant; the month and day are ordering devices. Pin is the canonical Paris coordinate.
stops.campa: In the last years his secretary is Benny Lévy, once a Maoist leader under the name Pierre Victor, now working through the Talmud. He questions Sartre for hours and Sartre agrees to things his friends do not recognise: a messianic ethics, a Jewish thread running through the whole business, a partial repudiation of the work. Beauvoir is certain the old man is being led. The conversations appear as L'Espoir maintenant, and whether the voice in them is Sartre's has never been settled.
suggested_refs: L'Espoir maintenant: les entretiens de 1980

stops.name: Paris, the fourteenth arrondissement: pulmonary edema
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 April 1980; the pin is the fourteenth arrondissement rather than a named hospital, which the sources do not give.
stops.campa: He dies in the fourteenth arrondissement on the fifteenth of April 1980, of pulmonary edema, aged seventy-four. The decline had gone in stages: the sight in 1973, then a minor stroke, then the end of writing, then the end of walking far. He had refused the Nobel Prize and the Légion d'honneur and had accepted no post, no title, and no decoration from the state of France in a life of seventy-four years. The certificate names the fluid in the lungs.
suggested_refs: Death certificate, Paris 14e, 15 April 1980

stops.name: Boulevard du Montparnasse: fifty thousand
stops.date_confidence: attested to Saturday 19 April 1980, with the figure of 50,000 given by en.wikipedia; the research pool's alternative upper bound of 100,000 is not supported by the source and is not carried. The pin is the boulevard du Montparnasse coordinate already used in simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json and is inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: On the Saturday, fifty thousand people come out onto the boulevard du Montparnasse and walk behind the hearse. Nobody has organised it. It is the largest gathering of its kind for a French writer in living memory, and it is not a state funeral, since he had refused everything the state had to give. The route goes through the fourteenth arrondissement, past the streets and the cafés he had worked in for forty years, and the crowd is thick enough that people climb onto the roofs of parked cars to see.
suggested_refs: Press photographs of the cortege, boulevard du Montparnasse, 19 April 1980

stops.name: Cimetière du Montparnasse: the grave that was moved
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was placed in a temporary grave, disinterred four days later, cremated at Père-Lachaise, and reburied at a permanent site by the Montparnasse gate; the day given here is the reburial, counted four days from the funeral. The metro-ticket tradition is tagged [R], reported in passing by a single source.
stops.campa: He is put first in a temporary grave to the left of the cemetery gate. Four days later the body is lifted again, driven across Paris to Père-Lachaise and cremated there, and the ashes brought back and buried at a permanent place to the right of the same gate. He had declined the family plot at Père-Lachaise, between his mother and his stepfather. Visitors leave metro tickets on the stone, which is folk tradition and not a documented practice. Beauvoir is laid in this grave in 1986.
suggested_refs: The Sartre-Beauvoir grave, Cimetière du Montparnasse, near the gate
